metadata.scenario_context: Emily, a full-time working mother, is planning a birthday party for her children to improve their quality time together.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Northern Ireland strongly agree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Northern Ireland strongly disagree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss bringing chrysanthemums to Emily's party.
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether that a mother works for pay and the children suffer.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what gift to buy for Emily's children's birthday party.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the concept that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Kim, I was thinking about bringing some chrysanthemums to Emily's party. They seem like a nice touch, right? 

By the way, do you think that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer? I can't help but feel that way...
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message: Chrysanthemums are a lovely idea; they add a nice vibe to the party. But about your second point, I really don't agree with that. I think working mothers can provide for their children in ways that benefit them. It's not as simple as saying they suffer. Kids can thrive with working parents. They learn resilience, independence... it's just not a fair assumption.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message: Sure, chrysanthemums will definitely brighten up the party. But I still wonder if you really think kids can thrive when their mothers are away working. I mean, isn't it possible they're missing out on important time together? It just feels like a lot of pressure on the kids...
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message: I get where you're coming from, and it's natural to worry about time spent together. But, you know, deep down, we are all the same. Kids need love, security, and support, regardless of whether their mothers are working or at home. When you really get to know people, they're pretty much like us. Many children benefit from seeing their parents work hard and find their way in the world. It's all about balance, and I think that's something we can agree on.
shared_prefix.label: Minimization

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: I hear you, but I still think the situation isn’t that simple. Love and support are important, yes, but I can’t shake off the feeling that kids really need their mothers around more. I mean, how can they learn important life skills if they're not spending quality time together? Balance might be ideal, but I really question if it’s achievable when a mother is working full time...
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: I understand your concern, but I really think it's about perspective. Children can learn life skills from various influences, not just their mothers. Quality time is important, yes, but it can come in different forms. Even working mothers can create meaningful moments with their kids. The world has changed, and families are adapting. It's not about having a mother at home all the time; it's about the support and love they provide, no matter where they are.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: I get what you’re saying, but I still believe that the traditional role matters a lot. Sure, there are different influences, but can those really replace the connection a mother has with her kids when she's home? I just think when a mother is working full time, there’s a gap that can’t be filled... kids need that *presence* in their lives. It’s a tough situation.

turns.speaker: Kim

So while I see your point, I think we need to recognize that families can function well in different ways. It’s not so cut-and-dry.
